Cybersecurity is one of the areas I am most interested in. Along with web development, the cybersecurity courses were the ones I enjoyed most at university. I like the idea that every system has weaknesses, and that understanding how things can be attacked is the first step to protecting them. Inside cybersecurity, the part I find most exciting is digital forensics. In our Digital Forensics lab we worked with **Autopsy**, which is an open-source digital forensics platform used to examine disk images and recovered devices. What I find interesting is the **entire process**, not just one step. It starts from collecting evidence at a crime scene, carries on through preserving that evidence properly, and goes all the way to analysing the digital devices that have been recovered. Every stage matters. If the evidence is not collected and handled carefully at the start, the analysis at the end cannot be trusted. For me, forensics feels like solving a puzzle where the clues are hidden inside files, folders and data. You have to be patient and systematic, and you have to follow the evidence instead of jumping to conclusions. My interest in forensics is connected to things I enjoy outside of class. I love **crime psychology games**, and one of my favourite books is **The Silent Patient**, which is a psychological thriller. So I am drawn to the investigative side of things: figuring out what happened, why someone did something, and what the evidence really shows.

stack:** Python with FastAPI on the back end, and HTML, CSS and JavaScript on the front end. **What it does.** The Process Scheduling Simulator lets you simulate CPU scheduling algorithms from operating systems and compare them. It supports five algorithms: - **FCFS (First Come, First Served):** processes run in the order they arrive. Simple, but one long process can make everyone else wait. - **SJF (Shortest Job First):** the process with the shortest burst time runs next. It lowers average waiting time, but long jobs can starve. - **SRTF (Shortest Remaining Time First):** the preemptive version of SJF. If a new process arrives with less remaining time, it takes over the CPU. - **Priority scheduling:** the process with the highest priority runs first. - **Round Robin:** each process gets a fixed time slice (quantum) in turn, which is fair and good for time-sharing. **Why I built it.** Scheduling algorithms are easy to memorise and easy to forget. When you can enter processes and see the order they run in, and compare waiting and turnaround times between algorithms, the concepts actually make sense. Python and FastAPI do the scheduling logic, and the HTML/CSS/JS front end shows the results. **Type:** computer vision system. **Tech stack:** Python, YOLO (Ultralytics), ONNX, and a custom trained model file called **best.pt**.

chunks.section: My Study Notes: CPU Scheduling (the theory behind my simulator)
chunks.text: I wrote these notes while building my Process Scheduling Simulator. Writing them helped me understand the algorithms instead of memorising them, which is how I prefer to study. A CPU core can run only one process at a time. When many processes are ready, the operating system needs a rule for choosing which one runs next. That rule is the scheduling algorithm. Different rules give different results for waiting time, turnaround time and fairness. - **Arrival time:** when the process enters the ready queue. - **Burst time:** how much CPU time the process needs. - **Completion time:** when the process finishes. - **Turnaround time** = completion time minus arrival time. The total time a process spends in the system. - **Waiting time** = turnaround time minus burst time. The time a process spends waiting in the ready queue. - **Preemptive vs non-preemptive:** in a preemptive algorithm the OS can take the CPU away from a running process; in a non-preemptive one, the process keeps the CPU until it finishes. Non-preemptive. Processes run in order of arrival, like a queue at a bank. It is the simplest algorithm and easy to implement with a FIFO queue. The problem is the **convoy effect**: if a long process arrives first, all the short processes behind it have to wait, so the average waiting time can be high.

the simplest algorithm and easy to implement with a FIFO queue. The problem is the **convoy effect**: if a long process arrives first, all the short processes behind it have to wait, so the average waiting time can be high. Non-preemptive. Among the processes that have arrived, the one with the smallest burst time runs next. SJF gives the minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes, which is why it is called optimal. Its weaknesses: in real systems you do not know the burst time in advance, and long processes can **starve** if short ones keep arriving. The preemptive version of SJF. Every time a new process arrives, the scheduler compares its burst time with the remaining time of the running process. If the new one is shorter, it takes the CPU. This reduces average waiting time even further but causes more context switches, and starvation is still possible. Each process has a priority number and the highest-priority process runs first. It can be preemptive or non-preemptive. The classic issue is starvation of low-priority processes. The usual solution is **aging**: slowly increasing the priority of processes that have been waiting a long time.

priority number and the highest-priority process runs first. It can be preemptive or non-preemptive. The classic issue is starvation of low-priority processes. The usual solution is **aging**: slowly increasing the priority of processes that have been waiting a long time. Preemptive. Every process gets a fixed **time quantum**. If it does not finish within its quantum, it goes to the back of the ready queue and the next process runs. Round Robin is fair and gives good response time, which makes it suitable for time-sharing systems. The choice of quantum matters: if it is too large, Round Robin behaves like FCFS; if it is too small, the system wastes time on context switching. The idea of my simulator is to run the same set of processes through each algorithm and compare the results side by side: the order of execution (like a Gantt chart), and the waiting and turnaround times. Seeing the numbers change from one algorithm to another makes the trade-offs obvious: - FCFS is simple but can suffer from the convoy effect. - SJF and SRTF minimise waiting time but can starve long jobs. - Priority is flexible but needs aging to be fair. - Round Robin is the fairest for interactive use but depends on a good quantum.
